item.title: OpenFold3 biomolecular structure prediction model available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.description:
OpenFold3 biomolecular structure prediction model available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University have released OpenFold3-preview, an open-source, all-atom biomolecular structure prediction model. This research preview is now available for deployment through Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.

🧩 How it works

OpenFold3 predicts the joint 3D structure of molecules from their sequences. Its capabilities include:

  • Protein folding for multi-chain protein complexes
  • Folding of protein-nucleic acid assemblies
  • Modeling of protein-ligand complexes
  • Single-molecule structure prediction for proteins, DNA, RNA, and small-molecule ligands

⚙️ Key details

Computational drug discovery teams can use this model for target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Because structure prediction tasks can take minutes, the deployment utilizes asynchronous inference:

  • Requests are uploaded to Amazon S3 and processed via InvokeEndpointAsync.
  • The endpoint supports an invocation timeout of up to 1 hour.
  • Results or error details are written back to a user-specified S3 location.
  • The system handles internal request queuing and scales to zero instances when the queue is empty to avoid idle costs.

🚀 Availability

OpenFold3 is released under the Apache 2.0 license, allowing organizations to inspect, fine-tune, and build upon the model. Users can deploy the model into their own AWS account using a few lines of code. The deployment runs in an AWS-maintained container with network isolation to maintain data privacy.

#OpenFold3 #SageMaker #Bioinformatics #DrugDiscovery #AWS

Source: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures | Amazon Web Services

item.title: PharmAgents2 Enables Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
item.description:
PharmAgents2 Enables Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery

PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end‑to‑end drug discovery, has been introduced, showing that a virtual pharmaceutical company can operate without human intervention throughout the research pipeline.

🔍 Overview

  • Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision‑making across a vast research space.
  • PharmAgents2 combines knowledge‑enhanced decision‑making with organized large‑scale exploration to address this challenge.

🧩 How it works

  • Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources; together with expert‑developed skills, it supports research decisions.
  • Self‑Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents that inherit research context and decision‑making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies.

📊 Benchmarks

  • PharmAgents‑Bench v.0.1 contains 121 questions spanning nine decision scenarios and three end‑to‑end tasks, assessed with expert‑defined process rubrics.
  • PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end‑to‑end tasks.

🧪 Real‑world validation

  • LpxH study: PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site, screened compounds against it, and identified a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding.
  • JAK1 study: The system prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity.
  • Proteome exploration: Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self‑Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome, identified a new binding target, and the interaction was subsequently confirmed experimentally.

💡 Significance

  • PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end‑to‑end drug discovery.
  • The work was submitted on 5 Nov 2026.

#DrugDiscovery #AIResearch #AutonomousSystems #PharmaAI

Source: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery

item.title: Google Antigravity’s Cheminformatics Skills Speed Up Lung‑Cancer Drug Design
item.description:
Google Antigravity’s Cheminformatics Skills Speed Up Lung‑Cancer Drug Design

Designing new medicines typically takes multiple days for a single iteration, requiring curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize.

🔍 Overview

  • Google Antigravity, equipped with new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows.
  • In a real‑world lung cancer treatment scenario, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour.

🧩 How it works

  • Division of labour: the language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations.
  • Data integration: built on RDKit and connectors to curated resources from ChEMBL and PubChem, the skills unify millions of structures from journal articles and vendor catalogs and encode domain best practices.
  • Interactive workbench: the agent extracts molecules from literature, associates them with reported data, launches an interactive viewer with customizable scatter plots (e.g., potency vs. rotatable bonds, colored by macrocycle status).

⚙️ Key details

  • Rigidification: adding a second bond to tie two substructures sharply limits conformational freedom, “paying the entropic cost in advance” and can dramatically boost potency.
  • Case study: crizotinib (first‑generation TKI) has five major rotatable bonds; lorlatinib (third‑generation TKI) is cyclized to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero, leading to higher potency.
  • Matched molecular pair analysis compared many pairs that differ by cyclization; results show cyclization reduces rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency.
  • The agent also built a large number of potency models using varying feature sets and model architectures, validated them on a held‑out set.

💡 Why it matters

  • Chemistry records are rich but error‑prone; a single atom or bond change describes a different compound, making accuracy essential.
  • By handling data wrangling and orchestration, the Cheminformatics Skills let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than manual preprocessing.
  • Accelerating the workflow from days to an hour opens the possibility of faster iteration cycles in medicinal chemistry.

#AI #Cheminformatics #DrugDiscovery #MachineLearning

Source: Agentic Cheminformatics with Google Antigravity

item.title: Citrini and Anthropic Test Claude on Scorpion Antivenom Design
item.description:
Citrini and Anthropic Test Claude on Scorpion Antivenom Design

An investment research firm wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development. They teamed up with Anthropic to see whether an unreleased version of Claude could make scorpion antivenom. The effort did not produce a drug.

🔍 Overview

  • Investment research firm (Citrini Research) wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development.
  • Partnered with Anthropic, weeks before its IPO, to access an unreleased Claude model.
  • Goal: use Claude to design proteins for a scorpion antivenom.

🧪 Experiment Design

  • Team built a 35‑page prompt and launched about 300 subagents to discover suitable proteins.
  • Anthropic reported Claude generated nearly 320,000 candidates, narrowed to 180 designs after discarding those resembling known toxins or existing proteins.
  • Anthropic added 31 designs, total 211.
  • Process took 64 hours.
  • Compute and token bill just shy of $50,000, covered by Anthropic.
  • Designs sent to Swiss biotech Adaptyv Bio and US‑based Twist Biosciences for testing, costing about $150,000.

⚙️ Results

  • Seventeen proteins passed muster, collectively binding to four of the five scorpion toxins the team hoped to target.
  • No protein bound more than a single toxin.
  • Binding to a toxin does not mean the protein can neutralize it; Citrini notes “no experiment has yet tested whether they actually stopped the toxin working.”
  • Experts tell The Verge the AI “couldn’t” make a drug and “came up with some promising starting points, but nothing close to an actual drug.”

💭 Takeaways

  • Citrini admitted “none of us could claim to know anything about AI as it related to biology.”
  • The experiment shows that, as of now, Claude could not create a functional antivenom from scratch.

#AI #DrugDiscovery #Anthropic #Citrini

Source: Claude did not invent scorpion antivenom

item.title: NVIDIA releases RFD4-Proteina, an open BioNeMo model for joint protein sequence and structure design
item.description:
NVIDIA releases RFD4-Proteina, an open BioNeMo model for joint protein sequence and structure design

NVIDIA released RFD4-Proteina, an open BioNeMo model co-developed with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, that jointly designs protein sequences and all-atom structures using reward-guided inference-time search.

🔍 Overview

  • Co-developed with Institute for Protein Design at UW School of Medicine.
  • Uses patterns learned from nature to navigate protein design space.
  • Co-designs sequences and all-atom structures.
  • Employs reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on promising candidates.

🧩 How it works

  • Combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables.
  • Autoencoder decoder outputs sequence and all-atom structure together, removing need for separate inverse-folding step (e.g., ProteinMPNN).
  • During inference-time reasoning search, model denoises generation trajectories, scores designs, retains/branches promising partial states, continues until criteria met.
  • Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence.
  • Uses residue-level latent representation (vs atom-level) to avoid memory blow-up.
  • Diffusion process engineered to cut sampling steps from ~400 (Proteina-Complexa) to ~60, focusing compute where reasoning matters.
  • Inference-time search accelerated via CUDA-accelerated oracles (OF3, physics methods like tmol).
  • Model and kernels co-designed with cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed/scalability.
  • AtomWorks provides molecular data layer for structure preparation and design annotations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supports Linux GPU host, Python 3.12; follow repo setup guide, need supported NVIDIA GPU.
  • Self-host requirements: x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting NIM prerequisites, Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, NGC API key.
  • NIM API endpoint (not for production): HTTP via build.nvidia.com, Shell/Python scripts, no local GPU/model install.
  • Accepts annotated CIFs or condition specification plus source structure.
  • Uses repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from PDB 5O45 as target; fix sequence/backbone, allow side-chain repack, direct binder generation to hotspot atoms Tyr56, Met115, Tyr123.
  • Generated binder length 100–150 residues, free sequence and coordinates.
  • Install repo environment with current uv release (validated 0.12.24); update uv if present to recognize CUDA 13.2.
  • Setup caches Hugging Face model bundle including paired autoencoder.

🚀 Availability

  • Available as open model for training, inference, method development, direct control over sampling code.
  • Also available as NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with HTTP interface.

💡 Why it matters

  • Faster and uses less memory than prior RFD3 due to residue-level latent representation, reduced diffusion steps, CUDA-accelerated oracles, and co-designed kernels.
  • Enables efficient protein binder design with integrated sequence-structure generation.

#ProteinDesign #BioNeMo #NVIDIA #DrugDiscovery

Source: Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: BioDuro appoints Greg Makara to lead AI‑enabled discovery chemistry
item.description:
BioDuro appoints Greg Makara to lead AI‑enabled discovery chemistry

BioDuro, a global integrated contract research, development and manufacturing organization (CRDMO), announced on October 1 2026 that it has appointed Greg Makara, Ph.D., as Senior Vice President Lead Discovery Chemistry to strengthen early drug discovery capabilities.

🔎 Overview

  • The appointment supports BioDuro’s continued efforts to build a more integrated, data‑driven drug discovery platform.
  • It is part of BioDuro’s continued efforts to strengthen its early‑phase drug discovery and medicinal chemistry capabilities and integrate modern computational approaches more deeply across its discovery platform.

📅 Announcement Details

  • Location: Irvine, Calif.
  • Date: October 1 2026
  • Quote from BioDuro CEO Dr. Armin Spura: “This appointment builds on BioDuro’s broader efforts to incorporate AI and advanced computational tools into our drug discovery services.”

👨‍🔬 Leadership Background

Dr. Makara brings more than two decades of experience in drug discovery and chemistry leadership across pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and technology companies. His career highlights include:

Position Organization
Founder & CEO ChemPass
CEO & CTO (co‑founded chemistry service business) ComInnex, Inc.
Site Head AMRI Hungary
Leader, Target Validation Chemistry group Merck & Co., Rahway
Director (participated in ASMS screening technology ALIS) Neogenesis Pharmaceuticals

He has experience spanning library development, hit‑to‑lead and lead optimization, computer‑aided drug discovery and AI‑assisted drug discovery.

🤖 AI & Computational Chemistry Focus

In his new role, Dr. Makara will:

  • Lead the expansion of BioDuro’s computational chemistry, AI, and lead discovery capabilities.
  • Work across the discovery organization to support lead discovery projects and expand computational approaches, including:
    • Molecular modeling
    • Structure‑based drug design
    • Fragment‑based discovery
    • Virtual screening
    • Molecular design
    • Compound prioritization
  • Complement BioDuro’s experimental chemistry, biology, and DMPK expertise to help clients accelerate hit identification, lead generation, and optimization while making more informed decisions throughout early drug discovery.

Quote from Dr. Greg Makara: “BioDuro has built a strong foundation in chemistry, biology, DMPK, and integrated drug discovery, and I am excited to help further connect these capabilities with computational and medicinal chemistry. The combination of computational and experimental approaches can create a more efficient and informed discovery process. I look forward to working with BioDuro’s scientists and clients to apply these approaches to challenging drug discovery programs and accelerate the path from hits to optimized leads.”

🌐 Strategic Impact

  • The hire strengthens BioDuro’s integrated discovery platform with more powerful, data‑driven approaches.
  • Clients gain access to combined computational and experimental methods designed to speed early‑stage drug discovery.

#AI #DrugDiscovery #ComputationalChemistry #Biotech

Source: BioDuro Appoints Greg Makara as Senior Vice President | BioDuro

item.title: Prompt Engineering Variability Limits LLM Accuracy in Drug Toxicity Prediction
item.description:
Prompt Engineering Variability Limits LLM Accuracy in Drug Toxicity Prediction

In a newly submitted computer‑science paper (3 Sep 2026), researchers analyse how prompt phrasing affects large language model (LLM) performance for predicting drug toxicity.

🔍 Overview

  • Title: Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction.
  • Field: Computer Science → Artificial Intelligence.
  • Goal: Investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction.

📊 Why drug toxicity prediction matters

  • Clinical trials in the UK can cost up to £1.3 million.
  • Approximately 90 % of drug candidates fail.
  • Toxicity is a major contributing factor to these failures.
  • Testing is both time‑ and cost‑intensive.

🛠️ Methodology

  • LLMs were prompted to identify chemical properties relevant to toxicity.
  • Prompts were varied to explore three dimensions:
    • Job role
    • Prompt structuring
    • Rule interpretation
  • The identified features were used to generate datasets that were then fed to traditional machine‑learning algorithms.

📈 Findings

  • Natural variance inherent in LLM outputs exceeds any performance gain from fine‑tuning prompts.
  • Substantial performance improvements were observed when chemoinformatic code extracted features, rather than using LLM‑generated values.
  • The proposed analysis method can be applied to a wide range of prompt types across different bioinformatics areas.

🌐 Related resources

  • Platforms mentioned in the paper submission:
    • alphaXiv
    • CatalyzeX Code Finder for Papers
    • DagsHub
    • Gotit.pub
    • Hugging Face
    • ScienceCast

🚀 Applicability

  • The analysis methodology is positioned as a general tool for evaluating prompt engineering in bioinformatics beyond drug toxicity prediction.

#AI #DrugDiscovery #PromptEngineering #ToxicityPrediction

Source: Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction

item.title: 🧬 AI Agents Transforming Life Sciences: How Data is Powering the Next Healthcare Revolution
item.description:
🧬 AI Agents Transforming Life Sciences: How Data is Powering the Next Healthcare Revolution

𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆: At the 7th Annual AWS Life Sciences Symposium, industry leaders revealed how generative and agentic AI are revolutionizing healthcare innovation. This article explores how leading companies are unifying data silos, deploying real-world evidence, and implementing AI agents that accomplish in minutes what previously took days—while highlighting practical tools any organization can leverage today.

🔬 The AI Revolution in Life Sciences Has Arrived

When over 1,000 life sciences industry leaders converge to discuss technology’s future, patterns emerge. At the recent AWS Life Sciences Symposium in New York City, one message resonated across all 26 sessions: generative AI has moved beyond experimentation into delivering tangible results, with the life sciences sector leading this transformation.

The symposium revealed a pivotal shift—organizations are no longer pursuing AI initiatives for innovation’s sake. Instead, they’re strategically scaling proven solutions that deliver measurable outcomes in research, clinical trials, manufacturing, and commercial operations.

But what’s the secret ingredient behind successful AI implementation? The answer was unanimous: 𝙙𝙖𝙩𝙖.

📊 Data as the Ultimate Differentiator

“Your AI is only as smart—and as strategic—as the data behind it.”

This statement encapsulates perhaps the most critical insight from the symposium. Companies achieving breakthroughs aren’t necessarily those with the most sophisticated AI algorithms, but rather those who’ve successfully transformed fragmented data into unified strategic assets.

AWS categorizes this data into three critical buckets:

  • Your existing data
  • New data you create
  • Third-party data

The symposium showcased how Merck Research Labs exemplifies this approach. Their team created a clinical data layer on AWS that consolidates clinical and operational information across studies onto a single platform, enabling automation that dramatically accelerates processes.

Another game-changing element is real-world data (RWD). Consider this striking statistic: 85% of FDA drug approvals between 2019-2021 leveraged real-world evidence. Despite its proven value, working with RWD has historically been slow and frustrating—taking up to four months to process. AWS partnerships have reduced this timeline to as little as two weeks.

📸 Imagine a data pipeline visualization showing the transformation from months-long processes to weeks

The collaboration between AWS, the Broad Institute, and Manifold AI further illustrates this data revolution. This partnership combines seamless data access with advanced analysis capabilities using AWS HealthOmics, Amazon Bedrock, and Anthropic’s Claude to power AI-driven research at unprecedented scales.

🤖 From Experiments to Excellence: Scaling What Works

A clear trend emerged from the symposium: forward-thinking organizations have moved beyond random AI experiments to strategically scaling successful use cases.

Johnson & Johnson’s approach exemplifies this shift. The company has pivoted to focus exclusively on their highest-value AI applications—a strategy that enables faster ROI, better resource allocation, and sustainable innovation.

Sanofi provided another compelling case study. Their AI-powered assistant “Concierge” delivers contextual answers about company policies and procedures. The impressive adoption rate—over 80% of Sanofi employees—demonstrates how deeply AI can integrate when it solves genuine daily challenges.

The most successful implementations target specific high-impact challenges. Working with PwC, AWS identified several use cases delivering significant value:

  • 🔍 Biomarker Discovery: AI agents mining literature and first-party data
  • 📋 Regulatory Amendment Analysis: Reducing costly protocol amendments through AI-powered feedback analysis
  • 🧪 Clinical Trial Analysis: AI-guided exploration accelerating insights
  • 🏭 Manufacturing Execution System Chat: Natural language interfaces extracting actionable intelligence
  • 💼 Sales Concierge: Supporting commercial teams with timely, relevant data
  • 🔐 Fraud Detection: AI-driven anomaly detection in drug pricing programs
  • 📈 Protocol Generation: Accelerating clinical trial design through AI-assisted drafting

To facilitate adoption, AWS has created the Life Sciences Generative AI Portal—a curated collection of over 40 generative AI demos and customizable prototypes already delivering value across R&D, clinical development, manufacturing, and commercial operations.

🧠 The Next Frontier: Agentic AI in Action

Perhaps the most exciting developments centered around 𝙖𝙜𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙘 𝘼𝙄—AI systems that can independently perform complex sequences of tasks to achieve specific goals.

Genentech showcased this potential with a striking example: A distinguished scientist completed a complex analysis of cell surface receptors in just 10 minutes using agentic AI—a task that previously required two full days of work.

To accelerate adoption across the industry, AWS recently introduced an open-source agentic AI toolkit built on Amazon Bedrock. This toolkit includes:

  • Research Agents: For target identification, biomarker discovery, and experimental design
  • Clinical Agents: Supporting trial analysis, protocol optimization, and patient stratification
  • Commercial Agents: Generating competitive intelligence and market insights

📸 Conceptual illustration of multiple AI agents working together to solve complex research problems

Publisher Wiley collaborated on an agent capable of searching full-text articles published under creative commons licenses. This agent delivers reliable, cited insights in minutes rather than the hours or days typically required for literature review—a transformational time-saving tool for researchers.

The toolkit’s architecture allows individual agents to connect with multi-agent supervisors using Amazon Bedrock’s collaboration capabilities, enabling developers to orchestrate across agents and build sophisticated workflows.

🚀 Building on a Foundation for Future Innovation

The symposium made clear that while technology continues advancing at breakneck speed, success depends on establishing a scalable, secure data foundation. This foundation enables organizations to adapt and evolve regardless of what innovations emerge next.

The life sciences industry stands at an inflection point where AI is transitioning from experimental to essential. Organizations that unify their data, implement strategic AI use cases, and embrace agentic capabilities are positioned to lead the next wave of healthcare breakthroughs.

What will your organization’s AI strategy prioritize in this rapidly evolving landscape? Will you focus on data integration, specific use case implementation, or exploring agentic capabilities?
